Eyes: Iris is uniformly deep dark brown to blackish-brown across all adult, immature, and juvenile individuals; consistent orbital pigmentation with no prominent colored eye-rings as a collective group feature. Face: Periorbital region is fully feathered without bare lores; loral tract and bill base are closely feathered with smooth plumage transition. The assemblage features subtle to prominent pale eye-rings, pale supercilia, dark auricular masks, erectile semi-concealed crown crests, and plain unpatterned facial planes. Adult facial markings are crisply defined, while juveniles show blurred, muted facial contrast and less distinct eye-ring delineation. Abdomen: Abdominal plumage is soft, fine-textured, and densely feathered; base hues include immaculate white, pale lemon yellow, creamy buff, and pale gray. Many species display unstreaked clean underparts, while some show subtle grayish smudging across the breast. Juvenile abdomens carry washed-out buff tonalities with faint andy mottling, lacking the bright saturated yellow or pure white underpart clarity of adults; undertail coverts are expansive, fluffy, and pale-toned. Wings: Moderately long, broad, and pointed wing structure adapted for aerial sallying, hovering, and short-distance flight. Upperwing coverts and remiges are dusky olive-brown or grayish, often edged with pale buff, whitish, or rufous fringes; several species show faint double wing bars. Underwings are plain pale gray or buff with neatly layered feather architecture, lacking extravagant bold patterns. Tail: Tail length varies from medium to exceptionally elongated; Scissor-tailed Flycatcher exhibits deeply elongated, forked rectrices, while most others have square-ended, slightly rounded, or moderately notched tails. Dominant tail colors are dark gray, blackish, olive, and pale gray; upper tail coverts blend seamlessly with rump plumage. Under tail coverts are soft, compact, and match ventral pale buff, white, or gray tones with neat layered arrangement. Legs and Feet: Legs are short to medium length, slender and sturdy, colored blackish gray, dusky brown, or deep gray. Feet follow standard passerine anisodactyl configuration with three forward toes and one posterior hallux; equipped with sharp, curved keratin claws for secure perching on branches, exposed snags, and open vegetation perches. Feet are entirely non-webbed, specialized for arboreal perching, aerial foraging, and open-ground stationary surveillance.

Body Size: All vireo species exhibit a compact, slender body plan with a body length of 12–14 cm (4.7–5.5 inches) and a wingspan of 18–22 cm (7.1–8.7 inches). They share a similar overall outline characterized by a relatively short, rounded body with a short neck and a moderately long tail, distinguishing them from larger songbirds. Juveniles are slightly smaller (1–1.5 cm) and less robust than adults, with a more tapered silhouette due to less developed musculature.

Body Plumage: Adults display a uniform, fine, dense plumage with subtle variations. The Black-capped Vireo has a solid black cap, white throat, and grayish-brown underparts; juveniles are duller with pale grayish-brown head and pale buff underparts. The Blue-headed Vireo features a vibrant blue head (ultraviolet-reflective in males), white underparts, and a pale grayish-brown back; juveniles are olive-brown with faint blueish tints. Philadelphia Vireo has a pale gray head with a distinct white throat patch and grayish-brown underparts; juveniles are duller with grayish-brown heads and pale buff underparts. Red-eyed Vireo shows a grayish-brown back, white underparts, and a pale grayish-brown head; juveniles are duller with olive-brown heads and pale buff underparts. Warbling Vireo has a brownish head, white throat, and grayish-brown underparts; juveniles are duller with olive-brown heads and pale buff underparts. White-eyed Vireo exhibits a pale grayish-brown head with a distinct white eye ring and grayish-brown underparts; juveniles are duller with pale grayish-brown heads and pale buff underparts. Yellow-throated Vireo has a pale grayish-brown head and a bright yellow throat; juveniles are duller with pale grayish-brown heads and pale buff underparts.

Beak: Short, slender, and slightly curved (approximately 10–12 mm in length), with a dark gray to black base and a fine, sharp tip. The beak is moderately stout for their size, with a slight downward curve at the tip, consistent across all species. No significant differences in beak shape between juveniles and adults.

Eyes: Dark brown irises, uniformly sized and positioned with minimal variation between species. The eyes are relatively large for body size (approximately 1.5–1.8 mm in diameter) and lack prominent scleral ridges.

Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-brown in all species, with a distinct white throat patch in adults (except White-eyed Vireo, which has a white eye ring). The base of the beak is pale grayish-brown, and special patches include a white eye ring in White-eyed Vireo (circumoral white ring), a bright yellow throat in Yellow-throated Vireo, and a pale white throat in Philadelphia Vireo.

Abdomen: Pale buff to white, with fine, dense feathering and a slightly rounded contour. The abdomen is uniformly pale without distinct barring or streaking, though juveniles may show faint, diffuse grayish-brown tones.

Wings: Moderately long (approximately 100–110 mm in length), with a rounded, slightly tapered shape. Wing feathers are primarily grayish-brown (base) to pale buff (distal), with a subtle, fine barring on the coverts. The wing profile is relatively short and compact, with a slight curve at the tip.

Tail: Moderately long (50–60% of body length), with a rounded, slightly flattened shape. Upper tail coverts are grayish-brown with fine, pale buff barring; under tail coverts are pale buff to white, often with a subtle, fine barring. The tail is short and stiff, with no prominent central tail feathers.

Legs and Feet: Short, slender, and bare (no feathering) with dark grayish-brown coloration. Feet are non-webbed, with three toes (hallux) and a slightly curved claw, typical of passerines. No significant differences between juveniles and adults.

Body Size: Large to very large pelecaniform waterbirds with massive, robust torso, broad chest, and bulky overall body outline; both species possess an elongated neck, large rounded head, and heavy-set proportions typical of pelicans; White_Pelican is marginally bulkier and taller than Brown_Pelican, sharing the same oversized aquatic bird body architecture with wide wingspans and compact abdominal girth. 
Body Plumage: Adult plumage presents species-specific base tones of immaculate white or muted dusky brownish-gray; feather texture is dense, coarse, and densely layered with waterproof contour feathers and soft downy underplumage for aquatic insulation; juveniles of both species exhibit duller, mottled grayish-brown plumage with faded, less saturated tones, lacking the crisp clean coloration of breeding adults, and show looser, fluffier feather texture until full maturation. 
Beak: Exceptionally long, stout, and massively robust with an elongated mandible and a prominent expandable throat pouch attached to the lower bill; culmen slightly decurved with a distinct hooked nail at the tip; bill color varies with species and breeding season but maintains the same oversized, thick-based structural morphology adapted for plunge diving and fish capture. 
Eyes: Moderately small relative to head size, rounded in shape; iris displays pale yellow, pale amber, or deep brown hues, consistent with pelican visual adaptation for aquatic and aerial foraging. 
Face: Periorbital region features bare, unfeathered facial skin with variable pale pink, orange, or grayish pigmentation; lores and bill base are largely devoid of dense plumage; both species lack bold patterned facial patches, characterized by smooth bare facial lores and gular pouch continuity with the lower mandible. 
Abdomen: Ventral plumage is either pure white or muted gray-brown with thick, compact feather texture; abdominal contour is full and rounded; underpart feathers are dense and water-repellent, with juveniles showing faint dusky mottling across the abdomen compared to uniform adult ventral coloration. 
Wings: Extremely long, broad, and paddle-shaped with deeply curved trailing margins; flight feathers are robust and elongated, adapted for dynamic soaring and gliding over open water; wing plumage is solid white or dark brownish-gray with contrasting black primary remiges in both species; folded wings lay flat against the bulky torso. 
Tail: Short, stubby, and broadly rounded in shape; rectrices are stiff and compact with uniform pale white or dusky gray-brown coloration; upper tail coverts align closely with dorsal body plumage, while under tail coverts are softer, paler, and densely downy in texture. 
Legs and Feet: Short, thick, sturdy legs with grayish, pinkish, or orange skin tone; feet are fully totipalmate with complete webbing connecting all four toes; claws are short, thick, and blunt, adapted for swimming, floating on water surfaces, and stable terrestrial perching on shorelines.

Body Size: Small to large piciform woodpeckers with an elongated, rigid upright body silhouette, stiff posture, and sturdy neck structure. Pileated Woodpecker is markedly the largest and most robust; Downy Woodpecker the smallest and most compact; Northern Flicker, Red-headed, Red-bellied, Red-cockaded, and American Three-toed Woodpeckers fall into intermediate medium body proportions. Sexual size dimorphism is slight; adults have firmer, more angular body contours, while juveniles appear slightly slimmer with softer, less rigid overall outlines. Body Plumage: Feather texture is dense, stiff, compact, and tightly appressed, with reinforced contour feathers adapted for impact absorption during trunk hammering. Adult plumage combines base tones of black, white, brown, gray, and barred buff, accented by bold red crowns, nape patches, facial markings, and solid monochromatic head coloration. Many species feature distinct horizontal barring, vertical spotting, or clean unmarked patches across mantle and underparts. Juvenile and immature plumage is duller, muted, with blurred barring, reduced red pigmentation, and lack of crisp adult head markings; they attain full adult coloration and patterning through successive annual molts. Beak: Chisel-shaped, robust, elongated bill with straight culmen, broad sturdy base, and sharp pointed cutting tip; structurally reinforced for excavating bark, drilling wood, and probing insect larvae. Bill stoutness varies interspecifically: larger species possess thicker, longer bills, while smaller woodpeckers have shorter, more delicate chisels. Bill color ranges from solid dusky black, grayish horn to pale slate; keratin texture is dense and wear-resistant. Eyes: Iris is uniformly deep dark brown to blackish-brown across all adults, immatures, and juveniles; orbital area is well-defined, with consistent pigmentation and no prominent eye rings, maintaining strong contrast against facial plumage patches. Face: Periorbital region is fully densely feathered without bare skin; lores and bill base are closely feathered with tight plumage integration. The group exhibits diagnostic facial traits including bright red crowns, nape crescent patches, small red cockades, solid red full heads, dark facial masks, and plain unpatterned lores. Adult facial markings are sharp and well-demarcated; juveniles show faded red accents, blurred boundaries, and absent or reduced nuptial head patches. Abdomen: Abdominal plumage is dense, firm, and neatly layered; base coloration spans clean white, creamy buff, pale gray, tawny brown, and warm tan. Several species display fine dark spotting, bold barring, or uniform unstreaked ventral plumage. Juvenile abdomens carry muted washed-out tones with softer, less defined spotting and barring compared to the crisply patterned underparts of adults; undertail coverts are compact, stiff-textured, and match ventral ground color. Wings: Moderately long, broad, and rounded wing shape adapted for bounding undulating flight and short-distance arboreal movement. Upperwing coverts and remiges are patterned with black, white, brown, and buff barring or solid dark tones; flight feathers are sturdy and reinforced. Underwings are plain pale buff or gray with neat layered feather structure, lacking extravagant contrasting patterns. Tail: Medium-length, stiff, wedge-shaped tail with rigid pointed rectrices specialized as a prop for vertical trunk clinging. Tail plumage features black, dark brown, and white barring or solid dark coloration. Upper tail coverts blend seamlessly with rump plumage; under tail coverts are short, dense, and tightly arranged, supporting stable vertical perching posture. Legs and Feet: Legs are short, sturdy, and muscular, colored dusky gray or blackish. Feet exhibit zygodactyl arrangement with two toes forward and two toes backward; equipped with large, sharply curved, robust keratin claws adapted for gripping tree bark, trunks, and vertical wooden substrates. Feet are entirely non-webbed, perfectly specialized for arboreal climbing, trunk clinging, and upright foraging posture.

Body Size: Small to medium-sized aquatic grebes of Podicipedidae, possessing a compact, streamlined, fusiform body with a notably low-slung torso adapted for aquatic diving. Western Grebe is markedly larger and more elongated than the smaller Eared Grebe, Horned Grebe, and Pied-billed Grebe. All species exhibit rounded chest and tapered hindquarters; sexual size dimorphism is minimal, adults appear fuller and more robust, while juveniles are slimmer with a more delicate overall silhouette. Body Plumage: Feather texture is exceptionally dense, silky, waterproof, and tightly furled, providing superior insulation and buoyancy. Basic non-breeding plumage is dominated by dark dusky gray, blackish upperparts and clean white to pale gray underparts; breeding adults develop rich saturated rusty rufous, black, and golden ornamental head plumes and intensified tonal contrast. Juvenile plumage is muted pale gray and off-white with duller, washed-out upperpart tones, lacking the vibrant breeding coloration and elaborate head filoplumes of mature adults; plumage is non-iridescent with smooth layering across mantle and flanks. Beak: Bill is moderately short to elongated, slender to moderately stout, sharply pointed with straight culmen and fine tip; Pied-billed Grebe has a shorter, thicker, more robust conical bill, while the other three species feature slender, attenuated piscivorous bills. Bill color ranges from dusky gray, black, pale horn to vivid yellow; some species display distinct pale bands or dark pigmentation on the mandible, structurally adapted for capturing aquatic invertebrates and small fish. Eyes: Iris is predominantly bright crimson red, deep ruby, or dark reddish-brown in adult individuals; juveniles possess duller brownish irides with less intense saturation. Orbital area is well-defined, with eye contrast prominent against surrounding head plumage across all taxa. Face: Periorbital region is densely feathered, closely appressed to the eye; lores and bill base are fully feathered without bare skin. Breeding adults develop distinctive erectile golden, buff, or black head crests, ear tufts, and solid dark facial hoods; non-breeding and juvenile individuals have plain, unadorned facial plumage with subdued tonal transition between crown, cheek, and peripheral areas, lacking ornamental plumes. Abdomen: Abdominal plumage is dense, soft, and downy-textured, predominantly immaculate white or pale silvery gray in non-breeding adults; breeding individuals may show rufous or dusky smudging on lower flanks. Juvenile abdomens are off-white with faint grayish mottling, presenting a less crisp demarcation between upperparts and underparts compared to adults; ventral feathering is highly compact and water-repellent. Wings: Short, narrow, and relatively pointed wing shape, optimized for underwater maneuvering rather than sustained flight. Upperwing coverts and remiges are uniform dark gray or blackish, with inconspicuous pale edging absent in most individuals. Wings are tightly folded against the streamlined body when at rest; underwings are pale gray or whitish with subtle layered feather structure, lacking bold wing bars or contrasting patches. Tail: Extremely short, inconspicuous, rounded tail with compact, fluffy rectrices, appearing nearly tailless in profile. Tail plumage is dark gray or blackish, blending seamlessly with the rump. Upper tail coverts are dark and tightly layered; under tail coverts are voluminous, soft, and white or pale gray, merging smoothly with ventral abdominal plumage. Legs and Feet: Legs are short, robust, positioned far posterior on the torso for aquatic propulsion, colored dusky gray or blackish. Feet are uniquely lobate-webbed with individual lobed membranes on each toe, rather than full webbing; equipped with small, sharp, curved dark keratin claws. Fully adapted for diving, underwater locomotion, and shallow wetland foraging, unsuited for terrestrial walking.

Body Size: Black-footed Albatross exhibits a medium-large body size (approx. 100 cm in length) with a robust, streamlined outline; notably smaller than Sooty Albatross (110–120 cm) but larger than Laysan Albatross (70–80 cm). Laysan Albatross is the smallest of the three, with a slender, elongated body proportionally more delicate than Black-footed Albatross. Sooty Albatross is the largest, possessing a powerfully built, elongated body with a distinctly broader thorax and longer wingspan relative to body mass.  
Body Plumage: Black-footed Albatross displays dark brown plumage on the upper body with fine, water-resistant vane feathers; juveniles are paler (olive-brown) with less defined markings. Laysan Albatross has a distinctive white head and neck in adults, contrasting with dark brown body plumage; juveniles are uniformly brown with duller tones and less pronounced white patches. Sooty Albatross features a uniform dark gray body plumage (slightly darker on upperparts) with smooth, dense feathers; juveniles are grayish-brown with pale underparts and less defined contrasts.  
Beak: Black-footed Albatross has a dark brown beak with a moderately long, slender profile and a sharp, black tip; the base is slightly swollen. Laysan Albatross possesses a short, stout black beak with a pale, whitish base and a distinct dark tip; the beak is relatively robust for its size. Sooty Albatross has a long, slender black beak with a pointed tip and a dark, almost black base; the beak is less robust than Laysan Albatross but longer than Black-footed Albatross.  
Eyes: All three species exhibit dark brown irises, with no significant variation in hue across age classes or sexes.  
Face: Black-footed Albatross has a dark, uniform face with no prominent patches; the periorbital area is dark brown. Laysan Albatross features a pale, distinct white periorbital ring surrounding the eyes, with a dark base of the beak and minimal facial markings. Sooty Albatross has a dark face with a pale, narrow periorbital ring and a small, pale patch near the base of the beak.  
Abdomen: Black-footed Albatross has a dark brown abdomen with a smooth, slightly glossy texture. Laysan Albatross displays a pale white abdomen with fine, soft downy texture. Sooty Albatross has a grayish-white abdomen with a matte, non-glossy texture.  
Wings: Black-footed Albatross has long wings (approx. 2.5 m wingspan) with a broad, rounded wingtip and dark brown primary feathers. Laysan Albatross has shorter wings (approx. 1.8 m wingspan) with a more pointed wingtip and white flight feathers. Sooty Albatross possesses the longest wings (approx. 2.8 m wingspan) with a deeply curved, narrow wingtip and dark gray primary feathers.  
Tail: Black-footed Albatross has a short tail (approx. 15 cm) with dark brown upper tail coverts and pale under tail coverts. Laysan Albatross has a short tail (approx. 10 cm) with dark brown upper tail coverts and white under tail coverts. Sooty Albatross has a short tail (approx. 12 cm) with dark gray upper tail coverts and pale under tail coverts.  
Legs and Feet: All three species have short, slender legs with non-webbed feet and sharp, curved claws; no webbing is present on any foot.

Body Size: Medium-sized seabird (45–50 cm in length), slightly larger than the common puffin but smaller than the herring gull. Streamlined, elongated body with a relatively short neck and robust thorax, presenting a compact, aerodynamic outline typical of pelagic species.  
Body Plumage: Adults exhibit a predominantly white body with a dark grayish-brown back, wings, and tail coverts; plumage is dense, slightly stiff, and water-resistant. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with pale streaking on the flanks and a distinct pale rump patch, fading to near-white in subsequent years.  
Beak: Dark gray to black in color, moderately stout with a pronounced, slightly curved tip (approximately 30–40 mm in length), and a sharp, chisel-like edge adapted for scraping food from rocky substrates.  
Eyes: Iris is dark brown to black in adults.  
Face: Periorbital area is pale grayish-white with a distinct dark brown eye patch; base of the beak is dark gray, and no specialized facial patches are present.  
Abdomen: Pale white with a subtle yellowish tinge in some individuals; texture is smooth and slightly glossy.  
Wings: Moderately long (150–170 mm), narrow and pointed with dark brown leading edges and pale white trailing edges; primary feathers are dark gray, while secondary feathers are pale brown with white tips.  
Tail: Short (approx. 100 mm), rounded in shape; upper tail coverts are dark brown with pale white tips, while under tail coverts are pale white with dark brown margins.  
Legs and Feet: Dark gray to black in color; legs are moderately slender with slightly webbed feet (reduced webbing) and sharp, curved claws adapted for gripping rocky surfaces.

Body Size: Medium-sized marine cormorants of the Phalacrocoracidae family, exhibiting an elongated, streamlined fusiform body with a long neck and robust chested torso. Brandt Cormorant is the largest and bulkiest among the three, while Pelagic Cormorant is the smallest and most delicately framed; Red-faced Cormorant occupies an intermediate size. Sexual size dimorphism is slight, with adult males marginally larger and more robust than females; juveniles possess slimmer builds and softer body contours compared to mature adults. Body Plumage: Adult breeding plumage is dominated by deep glossy black, charcoal, and bluish-green iridescent tonalities across the head, mantle, and entire body; feather texture is dense, stiff, tightly packed, and water-resistant with prominent metallic sheen on contour feathers. Non-breeding adults retain dark base plumage but display subdued iridescence and lack ornamental nuptial plumes. Juvenile and immature individuals exhibit dull brownish-black, sooty gray, and matte dark brown plumage with faint pale mottling on underparts, entirely lacking the vibrant iridescence and delicate filamentous breeding plumes of definitive adults. Beak: Moderately long, slender to moderately stout hooked bill with a sharply curved tomial tip and straight culmen; basal portion is robust, tapering gradually to the terminal hook adapted for piscivory. Bill coloration varies from dusky gray and pale horn to yellowish or reddish pigmentation at the base; all species feature a distinct nasal groove and compact keratinous structure suited for seizing and holding slippery aquatic prey. Eyes: Iris is typically deep emerald green, turquoise, or dark brownish-green in adult individuals; juveniles display duller dark brown irides with reduced chromatic saturation. Orbital contrast is pronounced against dark head plumage and bare facial skin in breeding adults. Face: Periorbital and loral regions feature prominent bare, unfeathered facial skin with vivid reddish, carmine, or dusky tonalities in breeding adults; bill base is framed by fleshy bare skin rather than dense feathering. Nuptial plumage includes delicate white filamentous crests or lateral head plumes in some taxa; non-breeding and juvenile individuals have duller, less vivid bare facial skin and lack ornamental head plumes. Abdomen: Abdominal plumage is stiff, dense, and closely appressed; adults are uniformly glossy black or dark sooty gray with continuous iridescent blending from breast to vent. Juvenile abdomens are muted brownish-black with faint pale gray or buff mottling and a matte finish, lacking the sleek iridescence of adults. Undertail coverts are short, compact, and match ventral dark body tones with tight layered feather arrangement. Wings: Long, broad, and pointed wing shape engineered for dynamic coastal soaring and sustained flight over open marine habitats. Upperwing coverts and flight feathers are uniform glossy black or dark charcoal with subtle iridescent greenish-blue marginal sheen; underwings are plain dark sooty gray without contrasting patches or wing bars. Wings fold tightly along the streamlined torso when resting or floating on water. Tail: Moderately long, wedge-shaped or graduated tail with stiff, rigid rectrices. Tail plumage is solid glossy black matching body coloration. Upper tail coverts blend seamlessly with rump plumage in dark iridescent tones; under tail coverts are small, dense, and uniformly dark, maintaining sleek ventral contouring. Legs and Feet: Legs are short, sturdy, thick-set, and positioned posteriorly on the torso, colored dark gray, black, or fleshy red in breeding adults. Feet exhibit fully totipalmate webbing with all four toes interconnected by broad membranes; equipped with strong, sharp, curved black keratin claws for clinging to rocky coastal cliffs and intertidal substrates. Fully adapted for aquatic diving, surface swimming, and vertical cliff perching.

Body Size: The male Augustus frigatebird (Fregata magnificens) attains a body length of 60–70 cm (24–28 in) with a wingspan exceeding 1.5 m (5 ft). It exhibits a slender, streamlined body outline characteristic of frigatebirds, significantly smaller than the closely related sooty frigatebird (Fregata martens) but proportionally more robust than the lesser frigatebird (Fregata ariel) in the same ecological niche. This size facilitates exceptional aerial agility and long-distance soaring.

Body Plumage: Adults display a vivid crimson to deep red plumage on the upper breast and chest, transitioning to a pale, almost whitish base on the lower chest and abdomen. The plumage is smooth and glossy, with fine, interlocking barbules typical of frigatebirds. Juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with pale streaking on the flanks and a dull, unmarked head, lacking the vivid red coloration and exhibiting a more matte texture compared to the glossy, iridescent adult plumage.

Beak: The beak is long, slender, and sharply recurved with a distinct, pointed tip. It is predominantly black in color, with a pale, almost ivory base on the lower mandible that becomes progressively darker toward the tip. The beak is not webbed, consistent with its specialized aerial foraging behavior.

Eyes: The iris is a deep, uniform brown, lacking any distinct color variation or reflective properties.

Face: The periorbital area (around the eyes) is pale, almost whitish, forming a distinct eye patch that contrasts sharply with the dark beak base. The base of the beak is dark brown, and there are no specialized facial patches beyond the pale eye region.

Abdomen: The abdomen is predominantly white with a faint, pale brownish tinge along the ventral margin. The texture is smooth and unfeathered in the central region, typical of frigatebirds.

Wings: The wings are exceptionally long (exceeding 1.5 m) and narrow, with a pointed, angular shape. The primary feathers are dark brown to black, while the secondary feathers are pale grayish-brown with a subtle, pale terminal band. The wings are held in a characteristic "V" shape during flight.

Tail: The tail is short (approximately 15–20 cm) and relatively stiff, with dark brown upper tail coverts and pale white under tail coverts. The tail lacks a distinct central pair of feathers and is generally held relatively flat during flight.

Legs and Feet: The legs are slender and relatively short, with sharp, pointed claws. The feet are unwebbed and adapted for perching on low vegetation or rocks, not for swimming or aquatic locomotion. The coloration is dark brown to black.
